spark.summary: A stateful proxy that monitors downstream failures and slow calls over a sliding window, tripping open to fail fast in microseconds instead of letting 2,000ms+ timeouts exhaust caller thread pools.
spark.keyTakeaway: Pair tight client timeouts with a circuit breaker so a degraded dependency triggers deterministic fallbacks instead of a cascading thread-pool collapse.

concept.whyItMatters: In microservice architectures, a single slow downstream dependency is more dangerous than one that crashes immediately. When a payment or inventory service hangs for 5 seconds per call at 100 RPS, an upstream Tomcat or Netty worker pool of 200 threads saturates in 2 seconds, causing unrelated endpoints and health checks to fail.
whenToUse: Synchronous HTTP/REST or gRPC calls to external third-party APIs (e.g., Stripe, Twilio, shipping carriers) where latency spikes are outside your control.
Internal service-to-service calls on non-critical paths (recommendations, loyalty points, analytics enrichment) where a cached or degraded fallback preserves core checkout.
Database or cache client wrappers protecting shared worker pools during failover elections or brief network brownouts.
whenNotToUse: Local in-process operations or purely asynchronous message-broker consumers (Kafka/SQS) where backpressure and dead-letter queues already isolate slow processing.
Critical idempotent writes with no acceptable fallback where failing fast is identical to propagating the underlying error, unless paired with an outbox queue.
Low-volume batch jobs where a 10-call sliding window cannot gather statistically meaningful failure rates before the job finishes.
keyPoints: Three-state finite state machine: CLOSED (normal traffic, recording metrics), OPEN (immediate CallNotPermittedException or HTTP 503 fast-fail), and HALF-OPEN (limited probe requests to test recovery).
Track both hard failures (5xx, SocketTimeoutException, gRPC UNAVAILABLE) and slow calls (e.g., >2,000ms) using count-based or time-based sliding windows.
Separate client-side 4xx errors (400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found) from infrastructure 5xx/timeout errors so malformed user input never trips the breaker for everyone.
Always configure a strict request timeout shorter than the upstream SLA; a circuit breaker without a timeout still blocks threads until the OS TCP timeout fires.
Combine with jittered exponential backoff and retry budgets (e.g., max 10% retry overhead) so half-open recovery does not trigger a thundering herd.

examples.title: Checkout Thread-Pool Isolation with Resilience4j
examples.scenario: An e-commerce checkout service calls a third-party tax calculation API with a 500ms p99 SLA. During a vendor brownout, p99 latency jumps to 8,000ms while checkout receives 80 RPS.
examples.outcome: A Resilience4j breaker configured with slidingWindowSize=100, slowCallDurationThreshold=1500ms, slowCallRateThreshold=50%, and waitDurationInOpenState=30s trips OPEN within 2 seconds. Checkout falls back to a local state-level tax table, keeping p99 latency under 45ms and error rate at 0%.

examples.title: Envoy Outlier Detection on gRPC Inventory Fleet
examples.scenario: One of 12 Kubernetes pods running the gRPC inventory service experiences a memory leak and begins returning RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and 5s hangs.
examples.outcome: Envoy sidecars configured with consecutive_5xx=5, interval=10s, base_ejection_time=30s, and max_ejection_percent=50 eject the unhealthy pod from the load-balancing pool within seconds, preventing single-pod degradation from poisoning 8% of all requests.

tradeOffs.pro: Small windows (e.g., 10 calls) or low failure thresholds (25%) trip rapidly during sudden outages, saving threads immediately.
tradeOffs.con: Too sensitive a threshold causes false-positive trips during normal GC pauses or isolated transient network blips.

tradeOffs.pro: In-process breakers (Resilience4j, Polly) support rich domain fallbacks like stale cache reads or default scores.
tradeOffs.con: Service-mesh breakers (Envoy/Istio) enforce uniform ejection across languages without code changes, but can only return generic HTTP 503s.

tradeOffs.pro: Allowing 5-10 concurrent probes speeds up recovery detection and avoids false re-tripping on one flaky packet.
tradeOffs.con: Too many probes against a struggling dependency can immediately re-saturate its cold caches or connection pool.

failureModes.name: Misclassified 4xx Tripping
failureModes.description: Counting HTTP 400, 404, or 422 validation errors as breaker failures causes a burst of bad client requests to trip the breaker and block valid users.
failureModes.mitigation: Explicitly configure recordExceptions / ignoreExceptions so only 5xx, 429, network resets, and timeouts increment the failure counter.

failureModes.name: Half-Open Thundering Herd
failureModes.description: When waitDurationInOpenState expires across 50 caller pods simultaneously, hundreds of requests flood the recovering service at once.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState to 3-5 per instance, add random jitter to open-state duration, and gate retries with a token bucket.

failureModes.name: Missing Underlying Timeout
failureModes.description: Relying on the circuit breaker without setting connectTimeout (e.g., 500ms) and readTimeout (e.g., 2,000ms) lets sockets hang indefinitely before ever recording a failure.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict socket/HTTP client timeouts lower than slowCallDurationThreshold and test timeout behavior in chaos drills.

failureModes.name: Retry-Amplified Brownout
failureModes.description: Placing a 3x retry loop inside the circuit breaker causes every failing call to multiply downstream load by 3x before the breaker trips.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap the Retry decorator outside the CircuitBreaker (or use a retry budget capping retries at <10% of normal traffic) so open-state rejections are never retried.

commonMistakes: Sharing a single global circuit breaker instance across unrelated downstream endpoints, causing an outage in /recommendations to block /payments.
Leaving waitDurationInOpenState at 500ms, causing the breaker to flap between OPEN and HALF-OPEN every half-second.
Returning silent empty arrays from a fallback without emitting a metric or degraded-mode header, hiding outages from on-call alerts.
Testing circuit breakers only with unit mocks instead of injecting real TCP blackholes or latency via Toxiproxy/Chaos Mesh.
Setting slowCallRateThreshold=100% without realizing a 99% slow-call storm will never trip it.

sections.content:
## The idea

A circuit breaker prevents cascading failures in distributed systems by wrapping remote calls in a stateful finite-state machine (CLOSED, OPEN, HALF-OPEN). Instead of allowing callers to wait on a failing or saturated downstream service until their own thread pools, memory, or connection pools collapse, the breaker detects elevated error rates or slow-call ratios over a sliding window and trips OPEN. While OPEN, calls fail locally in microseconds—either returning a degraded fallback or an immediate error—giving the downstream dependency breathing room to recover.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an Order API (200 Tomcat worker threads) calling a Fraud Scoring gRPC service. Normally, Fraud Scoring responds in 18ms (p99: 45ms). At 14:02 UTC, a bad index deployment pushes Fraud Scoring p99 latency to 6,000ms.

1. **Without a breaker**: At 100 RPS, all 200 worker threads block waiting on gRPC sockets within 2 seconds. Health checks on `/actuator/health` queue behind them, Kubernetes kills the Order pods, and the entire storefront goes dark.
2. **With Resilience4j**: Each Order pod wraps the gRPC stub with `timeout=1500ms`, `slidingWindowType=COUNT_BASED`, `slidingWindowSize=50`, `failureRateThreshold=50`, `slowCallDurationThreshold=1000ms`, and `waitDurationInOpenState=30s`.
3. **Tripping & Recovery**: Within 1 second of the spike, 26 of the last 50 calls exceed 1,000ms or hit `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. The state flips to `OPEN`. Subsequent calls immediately execute `fallbackScore()` (returning a rule-based low-value approval) in <1ms. After 30s, state transitions to `HALF-OPEN`, allowing 5 probe calls. Once 4+ probes succeed under 1,000ms, the breaker resets to `CLOSED`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Sliding windows, bulkheads, and decorator ordering
sections.content:
## Sliding windows, bulkheads, and decorator ordering

Modern libraries replace legacy fixed-interval counters with **count-based ring buffers** (last N calls) or **time-based circular buckets** (last N seconds). Count-based windows adapt naturally to low-RPS services without expiring prematurely, while time-based windows react faster under high concurrency.

**Decorator composition order matters.** Wrap calls from outermost to innermost as: `Bulkhead -> TimeLimiter -> Retry -> CircuitBreaker -> Downstream Call` (or `Retry` outside `CircuitBreaker` depending on whether you want retries to count as one logical attempt or individual breaker events). Placing `Retry` *inside* `CircuitBreaker` multiplies load on a dying service; placing `CircuitBreaker` *inside* `Retry` ensures `CallNotPermittedException` aborts retries or routes immediately to fallback. Pair breakers with a **Semaphore or Thread-Pool Bulkhead** (e.g., max 25 concurrent calls to Fraud gRPC) so slow calls cannot starve the remaining 175 threads serving `/cart` or `/health`.

## Resilience pattern comparison

| Pattern | Primary Goal | Scope | Key Parameters | Typical Implementation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Circuit Breaker** | Stop calling a failing dependency & fail fast | Per-dependency / Per-endpoint | `failureRateThreshold` (50%), `slidingWindowSize` (100), `waitDurationInOpenState` (30s) | Resilience4j, Polly, Envoy Outlier Detection |
| **Bulkhead** | Cap concurrent calls so one slow dependency cannot starve others | Per-caller thread/semaphore pool | `maxConcurrentCalls` (25), `maxWaitDuration` (50ms) | Resilience4j SemaphoreBulkhead, Hystrix ThreadPool |
| **Time Limiter** | Bound maximum wait time per call | Per-RPC / HTTP request | `connectTimeout` (500ms), `readTimeout` (1500ms) | OkHttp, gRPC `withDeadlineAfter`, Envoy `timeout` |
| **Adaptive Retry** | Recover from transient packet loss without retry storms | Per-idempotent request | `maxAttempts` (2-3), exponential backoff + full jitter, retry budget (10%) | AWS SDK Standard/Adaptive, Envoy `retry_on` |

## Failure modes

- **False-positive trips from 4xx errors**: Counting `400 Bad Request` or `404 Not Found` as failures lets a single buggy client trip the breaker for all tenants. Always whitelist or ignore business/client exceptions.
- **Half-open thundering herd**: Without `permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState` (e.g., 5) and jitter on the open timer, a fleet of 100 pods will simultaneously send hundreds of requests the millisecond the timer expires.
- **Over-aggressive slow-call thresholds**: Setting `slowCallDurationThreshold` too close to normal p99 (e.g., 50ms when p99 is 45ms) causes normal traffic spikes or JVM GC pauses to trip the circuit.
- **Stale fallback data masking outages**: Returning cached data indefinitely during an OPEN state without firing `circuit_breaker_state == OPEN` alerts leads to silent data staleness.

## Production telemetry and observability

Every circuit breaker must emit structured metrics to Prometheus/OpenTelemetry:
- `resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state{name="fraud-grpc", state="open"}`: Gauge (0=closed, 1=open, 2=half_open) driving PagerDuty/Slack warnings when sustained >2 minutes.
- `resilience4j_circuitbreaker_calls_seconds_count{kind="failed|successful|not_permitted"}`: Distinguishes genuine downstream errors from fast-failed `not_permitted` rejections.
- `resilience4j_circuitbreaker_failure_rate` and `slow_call_rate`: Plots proximity to the trip threshold during canary rollouts.
- Emit a `X-Degraded-Fallback: true` response header or span attribute (`fallback.used=true`) in distributed traces (Jaeger/Tempo) so engineers can immediately see why a request skipped the downstream span.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Isolate each downstream dependency and distinct SLA endpoint into its own named circuit breaker instance.
- [ ] Set explicit `connectTimeout` and `readTimeout` / gRPC deadlines strictly below `slowCallDurationThreshold`.
- [ ] Exclude 4xx client/validation exceptions from failure recording; record only 5xx, 429, timeouts, and socket errors.
- [ ] Pair the breaker with a semaphore bulkhead (`maxConcurrentCalls`) sized to `(expected_RPS * p99_seconds) * 1.5`.
- [ ] Place `CircuitBreaker` inside `Retry` (with full jitter and a retry budget) and configure `CallNotPermittedException` to skip retries.
- [ ] Wire `state == OPEN` and `not_permitted` rate alerts to dashboards and verify tripping behavior with fault injection (Toxiproxy / Istio fault injection).

interviewProblems.title: Third-Party Payment Gateway Resilience Engine
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Your e-commerce backend integrates with Stripe and PayPal for payment processing. During a payment partner outage, latency spikes from 200ms to 30 seconds per request, causing app server thread pool exhaustion. How do you protect overall checkout availability?
constraints: App server thread pool size: 200 workers.

dimensions.name: Short-Circuit Fail-Fast Strategy
dimensions.description: Tripping circuit breaker OPEN to instantly fail fast or route to fallback.

dimensions.name: Automatic Failover & Recovery
dimensions.description: Using Half-Open canary probes to test upstream recovery.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Wrap payment provider SDK calls in a Resilience4j circuit breaker with a 50% failure threshold and 5-second execution timeout. If Stripe times out, trip to OPEN immediately to route checkouts to PayPal fallback.
commonPitfalls: Allowing workers to block for 30 seconds on timing out calls, starving thread pools.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A stateful proxy that monitors downstream failures and slow calls over a sliding window, tripping open to fail fast in microseconds instead of letting 2,000ms+ timeouts exhaust caller thread pools.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Fraud gRPC applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Local Rule Engine.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Local Rule Engine experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Explicitly configure recordExceptions / ignoreExceptions so only 5xx, 429, network resets, and timeouts increment the failure counter.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Pair tight client timeouts with a circuit breaker so a degraded dependency triggers deterministic fallbacks instead of a cascading thread-pool collapse.
Avoid trap: Sharing a single global circuit breaker instance across unrelated downstream endpoints, causing an outage in /recommendations to block /payments.
Avoid trap: Leaving waitDurationInOpenState at 500ms, causing the breaker to flap between OPEN and HALF-OPEN every half-second.
When to reach for it: Synchronous HTTP/REST or gRPC calls to external third-party APIs (e.g., Stripe, Twilio, shipping carriers) where latency spikes are outside your control.
When to reach for it: Internal service-to-service calls on non-critical paths (recommendations, loyalty points, analytics enrichment) where a cached or degraded fallback preserves core checkout.

putItTogether.title: Putting Circuit Breaker Together
putItTogether.summary: Pair tight client timeouts with a circuit breaker so a degraded dependency triggers deterministic fallbacks instead of a cascading thread-pool collapse.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Circuit Breaker before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: A Resilience4j breaker configured with slidingWindowSize=100, slowCallDurationThreshold=1500ms, slowCallRateThreshold=50%, and waitDurationInOpenState=30s trips OPEN within 2 seconds. Checkout falls back to a local state-level tax table, keeping p99 latency under 45ms and error rate at 0%.
